title: Keep praying (Berakhot 33a)
hookLine: a snake bites Chanina ben Dosa at prayer; he doesn't stop, and the snake dies
tomorrow: if heaven holds everything, what's left for you to choose?

cards: A phone face down on the table buzzes three times in the middle of one sentence, and the sentence is gone. Now a different interruption. A sage named Chanina ben Dosa is standing in prayer.
Something moves in the dust at his feet. An arvad, a venomous snake, and it bites him. He doesn't flinch.
He doesn't stop. He finishes his prayer. Afterward, people go looking, and they find the arvad dead at the mouth of its hole.
So what kind of focus is that, and is it even wise?

teach.h: EVEN A KING, EVEN A SNAKE.
teach.b: The story sits on a rule. The Mishnah says: while you stand in prayer, even if a king greets you, don't answer; even if a snake is coiled at your heel, don't stop.
Prayer here is a conversation with God, and you don't walk out of that one to take a call. Then the Talmud tells about Chanina ben Dosa to show the rule lived.
He carries the dead arvad to the house of study and says to his students: it isn't the arvad that kills; it's sin that kills. Here's the part worth telling a friend tonight.
Right on the same page, the Talmud draws a line. A snake coiled at your heel, keep going.
A scorpion, stop. One classic explanation: a snake may not strike; a scorpion will. So the sages aren't praising recklessness.
They're teaching a sorting skill: what is only loud, and what is real danger. Most of what tugs at us in the middle of something that matters is loud.
The buzz, the itch to check, the thought about dinner. Chanina's story isn't asking anyone to ignore a fire. It's saying that the loud thing usually doesn't get to decide where your attention goes.

how: Jews say the Amidah standing, feet together, and the custom is not to interrupt it, not even to answer a greeting; Jewish law still says to stop for real danger.

o: staying in prayer through what's loud, stopping for real danger
a charm said to protect someone from snakes on the road
praying as long as you can, never letting anything end it

games.q: the rule and the story — tap the pairs.
p: a snake coiled at your heel
it isn't the snake that kills; sin kills

s: the Talmud says never to stop praying, whatever happens
on the same page it says a scorpion is different: you stop.
after the bite, the snake is found dead, not Chanina
people find the arvad dead at the mouth of its hole.
Chanina says his prayer worked like a charm against snakes
he tells his students it isn't the snake that kills; it's sin.

games.q: you're in the middle of telling your grandmother something hard on a video call. your phone lights up with a game invite, then the smoke alarm goes off in the kitchen. what does the snake-and-scorpion rule say?
o: finish the call no matter what; focus means ignoring everything.
let the invite wait, and go check the smoke alarm right away.
pause for both; any interruption could matter, so treat them the same.
games.why: the sages sort: a coiled snake, keep going; a scorpion, stop. the game invite is only loud. the alarm might be real danger.

practice: Choose one anchor: your breath, or a short line you love. Stay with it for the whole sit. When a sound or a thought pulls at you, notice it, name it, loud or danger, and come back without stopping.

wordCard.voice: Keep praying. Chanina's way: a snake at the heel doesn't break the prayer, and the sages still say stop for a scorpion.

orig.note: Hebrew: the arvad, the venomous snake in Chanina ben Dosa's story.

carryVoice: A line for the day: keep praying, and let the loud thing wait. Twenty-six of fifty in Berakhot.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (even if a king greets him, he does not answer; even if a snake is coiled at his heel, he does not stop)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33a (Chanina ben Dosa and the arvad; 'it is not the arvad that kills, sin kills'; a snake vs a scorpion)
